Judge tosses DOJ lawsuit that sought to block election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses
sources.text:
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed a Department of Justice lawsuit that sought to delay or block election results if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
The Justice Department wanted the judge to halt the certification of the election pending an investigation into whether voters who chose the other Dan Sullivan on the ballot were confused. Gleason said it’s not possible.
“The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” Gleason said in a 20-page decision Sunday morning.
The decision comes just two days before Election Day. An hour after it was issued, the Justice Department filed a notice of appeal. But at least for the moment, the decision closes the door on one element of the federal government’s attempt to involve itself in Alaska’s Senate race. The contest, primarily between Sen. Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, is one of a handful of toss-up races that will decide which party controls the upper chamber of Congress.
President Donald Trump, who said he ordered the Justice Department lawsuit, has claimed for months that a second Dan Sullivan on Alaska’s ballot could confuse voters and siphon votes away from the Republican incumbent of the same name. The president, as well as Sen. Sullivan and other Republicans, call the challenger, a retired teacher in Petersburg, a “sham” and a “hoax.”
The Justice Department case, filed Oct. 22, sought to block the state “from certifying any result that may be impacted by voter confusion.” It says confusion might be at play if Sen. Sullivan loses but would have won if votes for both Sullivans were counted for him. The federal attorneys asked for an order requiring the state to “preserve and segregate” ballots marked for the challenger Sullivan “pending an investigation” into whether the voter was confused.
The state, represented by the Alaska Department of Law, called the idea “half-baked” and said an investigation would be impossible, since ballots don’t have voters’ names on them and are comingled in the ballot box to protect voter privacy.
“The Court cannot order the Division to instruct poll workers to intercept and examine voters’ ballots before voters feed them into the voting machines to ‘segregate’ those that rank (challenger) Daniel J.,” the state response says.
The Division of Elections says the ballot already minimizes voter confusion. One candidate is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican incumbent. The other is on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. with no party affiliation.
Each state, according to the U.S. Constitution, has authority over its own elections. Alaska law has no prohibition on candidates running as spoilers, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled this summer that the Petersburg man has a right to be on the ballot.
Beyond the DOJ lawsuit, Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman said Friday the federal government is also investigating the possibility that a crime may have occurred.
“There is a surge in FBI resources, as well as resources in this office, to make sure that the election integrity remains in place,” he told reporters.
Heyman repeatedly referred to a New York Times report that seemed to substantiate what Sen. Sullivan and other Republicans had alleged for months: That Democratic operatives had an elaborate plan to recruit spoilers to the ballot, to help Peltola. The article said a fired Peltola campaign manager had text messages showing members of Peltola’s team were involved. The Times also quoted the campaign aide saying Peltola was aware of it, which Peltola denies.
While Heyman didn’t name any criminal statutes that might apply, a federal investigation into possible voter confusion appears to be underway in Southeast Alaska.
State Rep. Rebecca Himschoot, a Sitka independent, said she learned Friday that FBI agents paid a visit to at least two of her constituents, in Sitka and Petersburg, to see if they knew who they were donating to when they made campaign contributions to Dan J. Sullivan.
Himschoot called it “outrageous.”
“The people I serve are feeling harassed and invaded, and I guess I get a little spicy about it,” she said.
The challenger Sullivan has raised about $20,000 and is $30,000 in debt. Nearly all of his contributions over $200 came from people in Petersburg. Himschoot said she was among those who gave the Petersburg candidate a contribution.
“He is not supported by the Republicans. He is not supported by the Democrats,” she said. “He’s just a retired teacher who ended up with a Supreme Court case, which comes with legal fees. So a lot of us donated.”
A poll released Friday shows Peltola with a two-percentage point lead over the senator. It shows the challenger Sullivan taking more than 4% of the vote.

sources.news_title: Federal court tosses Trump lawsuit challenging Alaska Senate certification
sources.text:
Federal court tosses Trump lawsuit challenging Alaska Senate certification
A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit from the federal government seeking to preemptively block Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola from assuming office if she wins her race.
The Department of Justice sued Alaska last month, arguing that an alleged scheme by Peltola to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, an independent candidate who shares a name with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, would confuse voters.
Peltola’s campaign, the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee and civic groups including the League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause all filed motions to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the federal government lacks standing and constitutional authority to weigh in on Alaska’s elections.
They also said the court cannot grant relief because there is no legal way to determine whether a voter mistakenly voted for one Sullivan over the other without violating the secret ballot.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason reached the same conclusion, noting in an order “the absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot.” She also wrote that she “cannot grant the United States the relief it seeks because the United States has failed to establish the redressability prerequisite for Article III standing.”
Gleason’s opinion recounts Daniel J. Sullivan’s independent candidacy. Alaska Director of Elections Carol Beecher decertified it in June, later testifying that she did not believe he was running in good faith. State courts disagreed and restored his candidacy, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that ruling.
Alaskan election officials still took steps to distinguish the two candidates, listing their full names and labeling them “Incumbent,” “Republican candidate” and “Independent.” Alaska’s ranked-choice system lets voters rank both Sullivans, so they are not limited to a single candidate.
State officials and election experts also noted that nearly 60,000 Alaskan voters have already cast early or mail ballots, and there is no feasible way to reissue them.
The government’s one-sentence response said the state could segregate ballots and asked the court to allow a federal investigation into whether any voters were deceived. Gleason rejected that approach, saying the government offered no explanation of how ballot segregation or a law enforcement inquiry into voters’ intent could be carried out while preserving ballot secrecy.
Gleason also questioned the government’s constitutional basis, writing that the executive branch has no legitimate role in determining which candidates appear on Alaska’s ballots. The government said it was not seeking to change the time, place or manner of the election, but Gleason noted that its requests, including limits on certification, ballot segregation and an investigation of voters’ intent, all concern those matters, which are the state’s responsibility.
The lawsuit drew heavy media attention and concern from democracy advocates, but legal experts widely viewed it as exceptionally weak.
“Today’s ruling marks a victory for Alaska state sovereignty and Alaskan voters,” said David Becker, executive director of the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation and Research and a former voting rights attorney at DOJ. “By soundly rejecting the administration’s unlawful and now unsuccessful attempt to interfere, the court concurred with the State of Alaska that this is purely a matter of state law and that, under the U.S. Constitution, the federal government has no role in determining how Alaska certifies its Senate election.”

Alaska voters have the right to a secret ballot, she wrote, adding that regardless, such a move by the justice department would be too late as it is only days before the midterm election. Many voters have already cast their ballots in early voting and postal voting.

sources.text:
A federal judge on Sunday rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to stop Alaska from certifying its Senate election results.
The setback came just two days before the November 3 midterm election.
The Justice Department alleged that Daniel J. Sullivan, whom the administration labeled “Decoy Dan,” entered the race as a “frivolous candidate” intended to confuse voters.
“Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” the DOJ said in its filing.
But U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled that the administration lacked standing to bring the case. The lawsuit sought to require Alaska to set aside ballots if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost his reelection campaign to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.
The Justice Department is appealing the decision, although it remains uncertain whether the appeal will prompt any significant action before Election Day on Tuesday, November 3.
The Senate contest has drawn unusual national attention after reports suggested that Daniel J. Sullivan, a Republican whose name closely matches that of the incumbent, may have entered the race as a spoiler candidate to divide GOP support.
In its lawsuit, the Justice Department argued that the second Sullivan’s campaign sought to “dupe Alaska’s voters into believing that he is Senator Sullivan.” It asked the court to segregate ballots if Peltola prevailed. But Gleason said Sunday that there was no way to separate those ballots without violating voters’ privacy rights and the secrecy of the ballot.
A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska, showing both candidates named Daniel Sullivan
Voters cast ballots at a polling station in Anchorage, Alaska. The state’s U.S. Senate race has attracted intense attention over a second candidate whose name closely resembles that of the Republican incumbent

Gleason said the DOJ offered “no workable plan” for separating the ballots without infringing on voters’ fundamental privacy protections.
“The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling,” Gleason wrote.
“Simply, the Court cannot grant the United States the relief it seeks.”
The ruling comes as Sullivan and Peltola remain locked in a close contest that the Cook Political Report has classified as a “toss-up.”
The outcome could also shift control of the Senate toward Democrats if Peltola defeats Sullivan in his reelection bid.
Gleason denied the administration’s request to amend its complaint further, saying the move would be futile and would place an unnecessary burden on Alaska election officials just two days before the November 3 vote.
She also warned that subjecting the ballots to additional scrutiny could discourage people from taking part in the election.
The dismissal followed concerns Gleason raised during a hearing last week about the timing of the DOJ lawsuit. Alaskans had already begun voting, and the case was filed four months after the Alaska Supreme Court approved Daniel J. Sullivan’s appearance on the ballot, along with several distinguishing details intended to help voters identify which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent.
The decision represents the latest high-profile defeat for the Trump administration as it has sought, unsuccessfully, to expand federal authority over midterm elections.
Those efforts have triggered a wave of lawsuits from state and local election officials, who contend that the administration is unlawfully infringing on states’ authority to run elections under the Voting Rights Act and the U.S. Constitution.
The lawsuit is not the only action the Trump administration has taken in Alaska as it investigates the candidate known as “Decoy Dan.”
Last month, the Justice Department opened a separate criminal investigation into the campaign of the second Dan Sullivan.
The scope of that investigation remains unclear, but it is believed to involve, in part, allegations of conspiracy under a law dating to the Voting Rights Act era.
Peltola’s campaign and the national Democratic Party have denied any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy.

sources.news_title: Obama-appointed judge rejects Trump bid to block Alaska Senate results
sources.text:
A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s attempt to block Alaska from certifying the results of its closely watched U.S. Senate election if Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan loses.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled Sunday that the federal government lacked standing to bring the lawsuit, finding that it had failed to show that its alleged injury could be redressed by a court order. The Justice Department had sought to prevent certification while authorities investigated whether voters could be confused by two similarly named candidates on the state’s ranked-choice ballot.
The ballot identifies the incumbent as “Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent,” while another candidate appears as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” without a party designation. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, changed his voter registration from Republican to undeclared before the general election.
Read More on Politics
Gleason found that the government had failed to identify a workable remedy, noting that ballots already cast had been commingled and could not be traced to individual voters. She said requiring ballots cast for Sullivan Jr. to be segregated so voters could be investigated by law enforcement would “clearly violate Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot.”
“The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling,” wrote Gleason, who was nominated to the bench by former President Barack Obama.
Carl Tobias, the Williams Chair in Law at the University of Richmond School of Law, told Newsweek on Sunday that the most significant part of the ruling was Gleason’s finding that the federal government lacked standing because its alleged injury was not redressable.
“Without standing a case cannot proceed, so Gleason dismisses the case,” he said. He noted that Gleason also invoked the Purcell principle, under which federal courts are generally cautioned against making last-minute changes to election rules because of the risk of voter confusion.
Tobias said that because the government could not establish standing, Gleason did not need to decide whether the National Voter Registration Act supported the Justice Department’s case.
Justice Department Will Appeal Ruling on Alaska Senate Election
The Justice Department plans to appeal. In response to Newsweek’s request for comment, the department referred to a statement saying the court “dismissed the case on procedural grounds” but “did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”
“DOJ plans to file a notice of appeal. Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” the statement said.
The White House referred Newsweek to the Justice Department for comment.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the lawsuit over concerns about the two similarly named candidates appearing on the ballot in Tuesday’s election. The race also includes Democratic former Representative Mary Peltola and Republican Gerald Heikes.
Trump escalated his attacks on Sullivan Jr. on Sunday, writing on Truth Social that the “Fake Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., has DISAPPEARED” and claiming that “Nobody can find him, including Law Enforcement.” Trump accused Sullivan Jr. of committing a “Criminal Act” but did not provide evidence for the claims.
The federal government had asked Gleason to order Alaska election officials to preserve and segregate ballots ranking Sullivan Jr. so authorities could investigate whether voters mistakenly selected him instead of the incumbent.
Alaska’s Republican-led government urged the court to dismiss the case, calling the Justice Department’s position “meritless.” State attorneys argued that segregating ballots would be practically difficult and potentially incompatible with voter-privacy protections because ballots could show how voters ranked the candidates but not why they selected Sullivan Jr.
The state also argued that Alaska’s ranked-choice system allows voters to rank both men. If one Sullivan is eliminated during the tabulation process, ballots ranking him first can transfer to the other Sullivan if he is the voter’s next remaining choice.
Jamie Raskin Responds to Trump’s ‘Incumbent’ Comments
Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin defended the wording of Alaska’s ballot Sunday after Trump argued that many voters do not understand the meaning of “incumbent.”
“They identified the incumbent as the Republican incumbent. It could not be clearer,” Raskin said during an interview on NBC News’ Meet the Press. “Donald Trump says people don’t know the word incumbent. He should speak for himself, because the vast majority of Americans obviously do.”
While defending the ballot’s wording, the Maryland congressman criticized the alleged effort to recruit candidates who shared Sullivan’s name, describing it as “stupid politics” and “ridiculous politics.”
Why Two Dan Sullivans Are on the Alaska Ballot
The dispute over Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy began months before Election Day. The Alaska Division of Elections initially removed him from the ballot after concluding that he had filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead.”
A state judge later reversed that decision, finding that the removal was not based on applicable Alaska law and that the determination that Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy would confuse or misguide voters was not supported by a preponderance of the evidence. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the decision in June, allowing Sullivan Jr. to appear on the general-election ballot.
The controversy intensified after The New York Times reported that people working with Peltola’s campaign and senior Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee aides had participated in efforts to recruit Sullivan Jr. and other candidates who could draw support from the Republican incumbent.
Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC have denied recruiting Sullivan Jr. or other candidates. Sullivan Jr. has said that he entered the race because he was dissatisfied with the incumbent and wanted to give voters another option.
Criminal Investigations Continue Despite Lawsuit’s Dismissal
Gleason’s ruling does not end the separate federal criminal investigation or Alaska’s state investigation into the alleged candidate-recruitment effort.
The Justice Department has issued grand jury subpoenas seeking testimony or documents as part of its investigation. U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman has confirmed that a criminal probe is ongoing, although federal authorities have not publicly identified its targets or disclosed the potential offenses they are examining.
Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy also directed the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate the allegations. The department later confirmed to Newsweek that the Alaska Bureau of Investigation had initiated an investigation and would work with the Alaska Department of Law.
Dunleavy has suggested that the investigation’s findings could affect certification of the Senate election.
“If we find out there’s wrongdoing, and if that means that the certification then is stopped or changed, then that’s what happens,” Dunleavy told NewsNation on October 30.
Senator Sullivan said Sunday that he would accept the election results whether he wins or loses.
Democrats and Voting Rights Groups Welcome Dismissal
The DSCC called the ruling a victory for voters and accused the Trump administration of trying to subvert the Senate election.
“Today’s ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don’t like the result,” DSCC Executive Director Devan Barber said.
Barber also expressed confidence that Alaska voters would elect Peltola.
The NAACP, which filed an amicus brief in the case, also welcomed Gleason’s decision.
“This is a big win for the voters in Alaska and confirms that states run elections in our country,” NAACP General Counsel Kristen Clarke, a former assistant attorney general for civil rights at the Justice Department, said Sunday.
Clarke called the lawsuit a “baseless, eleventh-hour attempt to hijack this midterm election.”
Newsweek reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Steve Mollman.

JUNEAU, Alaska — A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.
Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democratic former US Rep. Mary Peltola in one of the country’s most closely watched races, with Senate control at stake. Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name. It was that candidate’s presence on the ballot that prompted Trump to push for the lawsuit out of fear he would siphon votes from the incumbent.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and as early voting was underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.
US District Court Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the order that the relief the United States seeks is “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
The Department of Justice, attorneys for the state and Peltola’s campaign did not immediately return messages seeking comment.
Senator says he expects ‘to lose a lot of votes’ to the other Dan Sullivan
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argued that the case lacked any legal basis and amounted to interference. The senator and his allies, including Trump, for months have portrayed Dan J. Sullivan as a sham candidate intent on confusing voters and helping Peltola.
Earlier Sunday, Sen. Sullivan told CNN that he thought the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot would affect the election.
“I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery,” he said.
He also said he doubted claims by Peltola that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters.
“There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” Sullivan told CNN’s “State of the Union.” “She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us.”
The senator’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Sunday court ruling.
In the week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in efforts to recruit the second Sullivan. Dan J. Sullivan in June, shortly after entering the race, said he’d had no contact with the campaign about running. He has not responded to multiple messages over the past few days.
Peltola’s campaign responded to the Times story by saying it had no involvement in the campaigns for either Sullivan: “I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said during a recent campaign event.
State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected Republican-backed efforts to block the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot on which he appeared as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Both Sullivans appear the same way on the general election ballot. Peltola placed first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan received about 2.5% of the primary vote, but that was enough to finish within the top four and qualify for the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election.

She also cited the Supreme Court’s Purcell principle, which holds that federal courts should generally not change election rules too close to an election.

Sullivan on the Alaska ballot, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. sources.text:
Federal judge rejects Trump administration attempt to pause Alaska’s US Senate election
An appeal is possible but could be moot if Sullivan wins or Peltola wins by a large margin; criminal investigations are continuing
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at a rally featuring President Donald Trump on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla. On Oct. 22, Trump ordered the U.S. Department of Justice to file a lawsuit that would prohibit anyone but Sullivan from being certified as the winner of the U.S. Senate election. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)
A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration that sought to block the state of Alaska from declaring a winner in the state’s U.S. Senate election.
In a 20-page order issued Sunday morning, U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason said the federal government failed to explain how it has the authority to bring its lawsuit.
“Therefore, this court lacks jurisdiction and the United States’ amended complaint must be dismissed,” Gleason wrote.
Less than two hours after Gleason’s judgment, the federal government said it would appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
Legal experts had expected the result because the federal government’s arguments were legally questionable.
President Donald Trump said last week he ordered the filing of the case, which asked a judge to stop the state from declaring anyone but incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan the winner.
Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins
Gleason is an appointee of President Barack Obama and the most senior federal judge in Alaska.
Polling averages indicate Democratic candidate Mary Peltola is slightly ahead of Sullivan in a race that could help determine whether Democrats or Republicans control the Senate.
A New York Times article on Wednesday said Democratic campaigners sought to recruit spoiler candidates in the race, including Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg.
Dan J. Sullivan and Republican Gerald Heikes of Palmer are the third and fourth candidates in the four-person Senate race.
The Alaska Beacon has not independently verified the Times’ reporting.
Peltola denied personal involvement after the Times reporting indicated she was aware of the recruitment, which involved an intermediary. Since the Times published its article, the federal government and the state have announced criminal investigations but have not said what crime may have been committed or whom they are investigating.
Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy had been challenged earlier this year in state court, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in his favor.
Peltola denies knowledge of spoiler candidate plan at Juneau rally
No way to preserve ballot secrecy, Gleason says
In written arguments filed since last week, attorneys representing the federal government had argued without evidence that Alaska voters might be confused by the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan and sought an order that would require the state to set aside all votes for Dan J. Sullivan, pending further investigation.
The state of Alaska, Peltola’s campaign, a national Democratic group and two nonpartisan voting organizations opposed that request.
In written filings, they said the action requested by the federal government would not prove any possible confusion.
“No pattern of ballot markings will reveal any voter’s reason for voting for Daniel J., regardless of how the voter ranks the candidates on the ranked-choice ballot,” state attorneys wrote. “And the ballot markings will be the only evidence of voters’ intent. Ballots cannot be associated with voters to allow the state or federal government to follow up with Daniel J. voters about their true intentions. Like every state in the union, Alaska protects the secrecy of the ballot by law, and such an investigation would require violating that secrecy.”
In response, the federal government could not explain how it would keep Alaskans’ votes secret.
“The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling,” Gleason wrote. “Simply, the Court cannot grant the United States the relief it seeks because the United States has failed to establish the redressability prerequisite for Article III standing.”
Federal attorneys suggested the state could segregate votes for Dan J. Sullivan to allow the counting of others, “but requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly (violates) Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot,” Gleason wrote.
Ordinarily, a plaintiff could amend a rejected legal complaint to show how it has standing, but in this case, Gleason said that would be unfair to Alaska because the election is so near.
As Alaskans vote, state’s top federal prosecutor confirms criminal investigation of Dem groups
Appeal is possible but may be moot
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which was named in the Times article as one of the organizations recruiting spoilers, had intervened in the lawsuit alongside the Peltola campaign and the state of Alaska.
“Today’s ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don’t like the result,” said DSCC executive director Devan Barber in an emailed statement.    
            
	
While the federal government has appealed Sunday’s decision to the 9th Circuit, action in that court may not take place until after Election Day.
If incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan wins the election, or if Peltola wins by a margin that is larger than the number of votes received by Dan J. Sullivan, an appeal could be moot.
In addition, there is some indication that the 9th Circuit may be unwilling to overturn the rejection. On Oct. 26, a three-judge panel from the 9th Circuit rejected an emergency order filed by the federal government against California elections officials. A lower court had also dismissed the federal lawsuit against California.
In that ruling, one of the concurring judges wrote, “On balance, given the record and because Plaintiff has offered no workable plan of any kind as to how the remedy it seeks could be accomplished in practice without potential catastrophic consequences to California’s ongoing election, the equities between the parties and the public’s interest do not weigh in favor of granting the requested relief.”
Through Saturday, almost 15% of registered Alaska voters had already cast ballots for the general election. Turnout is expected to be near 50%, based on trends over the past two midterms.
Correction: A prior version of this article incorrectly attributed a quote from a 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals decision on Oct. 26. The quote should have been attributed to one judge, not a three-judge panel in a ruling on an emergency order.

US President Donald Trump speaks with the media as he arrives at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida, US, October 31, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY
President Donald Trump’s preemptive legal challenge to the results of the Senate race in Alaska was dealt a significant blow Sunday after a federal judge threw out the Justice Department’s lawsuit, Politico’s Kyle Cheney reported.
Last month, the DOJ, at the direction of Trump, filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Alaska state officials from certifying election results if Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) loses his reelection bid. The DOJ claimed that voters could be confused over there being two candidates named Sullivan on the ballot.
In a court filing, the DOJ requested ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan — who’s running as an independent against Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) and Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola — be segregated. But on Sunday, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason rebuked the DOJ’s argument.
“Requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly violate [sic] Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot,” Gleason wrote.
As such, Gleason dismissed the DOJ’s lawsuit “without leave to amend,” meaning the DOJ cannot revise its complaint again in the case.

A federal judge threw out a Justice Department lawsuit on Sunday aimed at halting the certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race should Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan lose.
Sullivan, a key ally of President Donald Trump, is competing against Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola in a pivotal contest that could determine control of the Senate. Tuesday’s ranked-choice voting also features two minor candidates, one of whom shares the senator’s name.
The presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot led Trump to push for legal action over concerns that votes intended for the incumbent would be siphoned away.
Submitted less than two weeks before the election while early voting was already under way, the lawsuit demanded an investigation into whether votes cast for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were actually meant for the senator. State officials called the suit baseless, arguing it would be impossible to make such a determination without breaching voter privacy.
In her order, U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason ruled that the remedies requested by the federal government were "infeasible" given the high volume of votes already cast.
"More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," she wrote.
Peltola’s team and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee maintained that the suit lacked any legal standing and was a clear attempt at interference. For months, Sullivan and his supporters, including Trump, have framed Dan J. Sullivan as a decoy candidate placed on the ballot to confuse voters and assist Peltola.
Speaking on CNN earlier Sunday, Sen. Sullivan stated that he expected the second candidate's presence to alter the election outcome.
"I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery," he said.
He also voiced skepticism regarding Peltola’s claims that she had no knowledge of her top political aides recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race to mislead voters.
"There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her," Sullivan said during an appearance on CNN. "She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us."
In the final week leading up to Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was tied to efforts aimed at recruiting the second Sullivan. Shortly after entering the race in June, Dan J. Sullivan said he had not communicated with her campaign regarding his candidacy. He has not replied to recent messages seeking comment.
Addressing the Times report, Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement with either Sullivan's campaign, with Peltola stating during a recent public appearance: "I am not interested in tricking voters."
State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, previously threw out Republican challenges seeking to remove the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot, where he ran without party affiliation as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The senator appeared as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Both names appear identically on the general election ballot. Peltola finished first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan captured roughly 2.5% of the primary vote, which was enough to secure a top-four spot and advance to the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election.
Attorneys from the Alaska Department of Law representing state election officials had asked Gleason, an appointee of former Democratic President Barack Obama, to dismiss the case, describing the federal government's filing as "meritless."
State attorneys added that Alaska had taken "significant steps" to help voters differentiate between the two candidates, noting that confused voters could ask for assistance or read candidate background details provided in official state election booklets.
Republicans, including allies of Trump, also have a long track record of supporting decoy candidates in political races. The governor, a Republican, has directed an inquiry into the matter and raised the possibility of withholding certification if Peltola wins.
Gleason noted in her decision that the Trump administration’s attempt to halt certification directly conflicted with the Constitution, which assigns election oversight to the states. She also pointed to the Supreme Court's Purcell principle, which dictates that federal courts should refrain from modifying election rules shortly before an election.
On Thursday, the Justice Department expanded a criminal investigation into Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy, issuing several new grand jury subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the matter. FBI agents have also begun interviewing donors to his campaign to determine whether they were misled about the candidate they were supporting.

sources.news_title: Judge tosses DOJ’s attempt to delay Alaska Senate results if Republican loses
Judge dismisses Alaska Senate election lawsuit; DOJ vows appeal
sources.text:
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Department of Justice's extraordinary lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the Alaska Senate election if incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan loses, citing possible voter confusion from another candidate with his name on the ballot.
The ruling came two days before Election Day and two days after the U.S. Attorney for Alaska said ongoing criminal and civil investigations into non-incumbent Dan J. Sullivan's decision to run for the Senate.
The campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola, state election officials and outside advocacy groups had asked Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the DOJ's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage.
The Department of Justice quickly filed a notice of its intention to appeal the decision to the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals.
Peltola is locked in a tight contest with Sen. Dan Sullivan, whose winner will be determined by a ranked-choice system.
The outcome of the race is one of several contests that determine which party has a Senate majority, where Republicans currently hold a narrow lead.
Neither the other Sullivan nor the fourth candidate on the ballot, Gerald Heikes, is considered a contender.
But voters who rank them as a first choice could swing the outcome by ranking Peltola or Sen. Sullivan second.
Peltola's campaign has been accused of encouraging retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan to run for the Senate against the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Peltola.
Her campaign has denied those claims.
"No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on November 3rd so she can lower costs for Alaska's working families," Peltola's campaign said in a statement after Sunday's ruling.
"Alaskans will choose their next U.S. Senator – not Dan Sullivan or his DC allies," the campaign said.
In her 20-page decision, Gleason did not resolve whether another Sullivan had been recruited to confuse voters.
Instead, she said the federal government had failed to establish that it had legal standing to file a civil complaint to postpone certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan lost.
In that event, the DOJ wanted an investigation into voter intent and possible confusion from having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.
"The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling," Gleason said in her ruling.
She noted that early voting in the state was already underway, and that ballots already cast have been commingled in a way that would prevent officials from linking individual ballots to voters.
"More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote.
The judge also cited a Supreme Court decision that established the so-called Purcell principle, which "strongly cautions" against courts altering election rules on the eve of election.
She noted that DOJ claimed it was not seeking to alter the "time, place or manner of Alaska's election."
But at the same time, Gleason said, the DOJ was asking her for an order "preventing the State
from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan."
"These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska's election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the executive branch of the federal government," Gleason said.
The judge said she would not allow the DOJ to amend the lawsuit, which was revised last week to add a new legal claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim under the National Voter Registration Act. The amended complaint also added details of a New York Times article about the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan.
"The Court finds that further amendment would be futile because this Court lacks the authority to order that certain ballots cast by Alaskans be segregated so that federal law enforcement officials can conduct an unspecified investigation of the voters who cast them," Gleason said.
A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement, "The court dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters."
"DOJ plans to file a notice of appeal," the spokesperson said. "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes."
The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to the DOJ's statement.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the lawsuit, which was filed Oct. 22.
Trump argued that Peltola and other Democrats had recruited the former school teacher to run in hopes of confusing voters who wanted to cast their ballots for Sen. Sullivan.
Trump, in his first comments after the ruling, said: "So we have two Dan Sullivans. This is voter fraud at the highest level. But the Democrat candidate who is involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."
The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Peltola campaign aides and DSCC aides had been involved in efforts to recruit the retiree for the race.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied having any involvement in his campaign.
DSCC Executive Director Devan Barber said in a statement, "Today's ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don't like the result."
"We will never stop fighting back against the shameful, brazen efforts from the Trump administration and their weaponized Department of Justice to subvert the U.S. Senate race in Alaska, or any other election as voters reject Republicans at ballot boxes across the country – and we are confident Alaska voters will elect Mary Peltola to the Senate," Barber said.
Sen. Sullivan, in an interview on CNN before Gleason issued her ruling, said he would accept the election results if he lost.
But he also blasted Peltola's campaign and the DSCC.
"Recognizing they couldn't run on their record, so they had to cheat," Sullivan said. "I think a lot of Alaskans, even Democrats, are thinking she is not fit for office; she's continually lying to the Alaskan people, and I guarantee you she's lying right now."
Alaska election officials have pointed to steps they took to avoid voter confusion on the ballots for the race.
The ballots list Sen. Sullivan as "Dan S. Sullivan," with the words "incumbent" and "registered Republican" next to his name.
The other Sullivan is listed as "Daniel J. Sullivan," with no other words next to his name.
Election officials originally had blocked the retired teacher from the primary ballot. But a state judge allowed him on the ballot. Alaska's Supreme Court upheld that ruling.

sources.news_title: Alaska Senate race: US judge dismisses Trump administration's bid to block certification if Dan Sullivan loses
sources.text:
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a US Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block the certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.
The ruling comes just days before an election that could help determine which party controls the US Senate. Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, is facing former US Representative Peltola in one of the country's closely watched races.
The Tuesday election will use ranked-choice voting and also features two candidates who have done little campaigning. One of them shares the incumbent senator's name.
The Justice Department filed the lawsuit less than two weeks before the election, while early voting was already underway. It sought an investigation into whether votes cast for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were actually intended for the Republican senator.
Alaska officials argued that the lawsuit lacked merit and that determining voters' intentions would be impossible without compromising ballot secrecy.
US District Court Judge Sharon Gleason said in her order that the relief sought by the government was “infeasible” because many voters had already cast their ballots. Those ballots had been commingled to the extent that the identity of the individuals who cast them could no longer be determined.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified “investigation” of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
The lawsuit is linked to allegations that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola and her campaign were involved in recruiting a retired schoolteacher named Dan Sullivan to enter the Senate race, potentially confusing voters.
Republican Senator Dan Sullivan said on Sunday that he doubted Peltola's claims that she had no knowledge of her senior political aides' alleged involvement in recruiting the second candidate.
Republicans have long suspected that Peltola and her campaign were behind the other Sullivan's presence on the ballot. Their suspicions were reinforced by a New York Times report published last week, which cited interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, text messages and campaign finance documents. The report said an operative attempting to recruit decoy candidates had been paid by a group supporting Peltola.
“There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” Sullivan told CNN's “State of the Union,” two days before Election Day. “She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us.”
Peltola has denied any involvement in recruiting the other Sullivan. She has described the attention surrounding the issue as a “distraction” from the main concerns facing Alaskans, including high prices caused by the war in Iran launched by Republican Donald Trump.
Her campaign has also denied involvement, as has the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the national Democratic organisation focused on Senate races.
Before a rally on Friday, Peltola was asked whether someone from her campaign could have been involved in recruiting the other candidate.
“I have no idea,” she told KTUU. “I honestly have no idea.”
The second candidate is listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., while the senator appears as Dan S. Sullivan and is identified as the Republican incumbent. The retired teacher has maintained that he entered the race on his own accord.
Trump had directed his Justice Department to file a lawsuit seeking to stop certification of a possible Peltola victory. After the New York Times report was published, he also called for the Democratic candidate to be prosecuted.
Federal agents subsequently arrived in Alaska and issued subpoenas as part of the investigation. However, Republicans, including those working with Trump, have also had a long history of supporting decoy candidates in elections.
Alaska's Republican governor has ordered an investigation and suggested he may not certify a possible Peltola victory.
South Carolina Senator Tim Scott, who leads the Republican group focused on Senate races, said on NBC's “Meet the Press” that criminal charges could be justified.
"We know that it is criminal for candidates to work in collusion with other parties to confuse voters,” he said.
Representative Jamie Raskin, a Democrat from Maryland, said candidates sharing names with other people on the ballot was something that “happens all over the place”. However, he said promoting such a strategy was not something he would support.
“It’s stupid politics,” he told NBC. “Nobody would do that, and Mary Peltola has said she had nothing to do with it.”
Senator Bernie Sanders also weighed in on the controversy. The Vermont independent said on CBS' “Face the Nation”:
“What the Democrats did in Alaska seems to me to be pretty dumb," the Vermont independent said on CBS' “Face the Nation.” "It’s not illegal. It’s what happens in every election.”
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general, said he would “let the lawyers” determine whether any crimes had been committed. He also said he believed the second candidate's presence on the ballot would affect the outcome.
“I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery,” Sullivan said.
Asked whether he would urge state officials not to certify a Peltola victory, Sullivan initially declined to give a direct answer before saying, "I'm going to accept the results of the election.”
Both candidates spent the final days of the campaign travelling across Alaska's vast landscape.
On Saturday night, Sullivan handed out candy at a “trunk-or-treat” event at a recreation centre north of Anchorage. He joked that his costume was “the real Dan Sullivan.”

The district court found that the U.S. did not have standing because it could not demonstrate that the court could grant any relief that would not violate voters’ right to ballot secrecy, or be consistent with the Elections Clause giving the states the right to run elections (subject to congressional override) or be consistent with the Purcell principle on federal court orders issued close to the election.

sources.news_title: Judge throws out DOJ attempt to delay certification of Alaska Senate race
sources.text:
Judge throws out DOJ attempt to delay certification of Alaska Senate race
By Dan Berman, Tierney Sneed, Jeremy Herb, CNN
(CNN) — A federal judge on Sunday threw out the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to segregate ballots and delay certification of Alaska’s Senate race, the latest legal rebuke to a rash of Trump administration attempts to meddle in the 2026 midterms.
US District Judge Sharon Gleason said the federal government doesn’t have the standing to force Alaska to segregate ballots and that such a move would violate the right of voters to cast a secret ballot. Regardless, she added, it’s too late for the courts to force such a major change on the eve of an election.
The Trump administration in its suit argued the presence of a spoiler candidate with the same name as the GOP incumbent warranted a court-ordered investigation into the results if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan lost.
Gleason, a nominee of former President Barack Obama, wrote, “The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,”
The ruling is the latest legal setback for the Trump administration in its efforts to inject itself in to states’ voting processes in the final days of the midterm elections. A federal appeals court on Friday rejected a Justice Department demand that California election officials set aside ballots from 20,000 people the administration claims could be noncitizens.
The Justice Department on Sunday quickly filed a notice of appeal following the district court’s ruling.
“Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a Justice Department spokesperson said.
Trump said he had not heard about the ruling while speaking to reporters on the tarmac outside of Air Force One after he landed in Iowa for a campaign rally Sunday, but described the DOJ’s case as “one of the most meritful things,” and a “very important lawsuit.”
Meanwhile, the courts have also imposed restrictions on the Trump administration’s efforts to hunt for alleged voter fraud and on the DOJ’s threats to local election officials that they could face criminal penalties over noncitizen voting. A federal judge late Friday imposed a sweeping emergency order restricting the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from demanding that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters from voter rolls, or halt ballot processing.
US District Judge Trina Thompson, an appointee of President Joe Biden, also ruled that the Trump administration cannot “threaten, intimidate or coerce” election officials to demand changes in ballot processing procedures on claims voters are ineligible. The Justice Department has appealed the ruling.
New allegations in Alaska Senate race
The Alaska Senate race, in which Democrat Mary Peltola is trying to unseat Sullivan, was roiled this week by a New York Times report with new details about Democratic involvement in getting Daniel J. Sullivan onto the ballot in a race that could determine which party controls the Senate.
While the civil case played out, the Justice Department also accelerated its criminal probe into the alleged Democratic efforts, and the state’s Republican governor ordered an investigation, while suggesting he could oppose certification depending on the results of the probe.
Alaska officials, Democratic groups and nonpartisan voter advocacy organizations that all opposed the DOJ lawsuit argued the administration had no legal right to drag a federal court into a dispute over Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy that had been settled with state court litigation several months ago.
They argued the DOJ put forward no evidence that voters were confused by his inclusion — particularly as election administrators included several identifiers on the ballot to distinguish him from Sen. Sullivan.

sources.text:
By Nicholas Riccardi and Becky Bohrer
JUNEAU, Alaska — A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, the latest development in a ballot controversy that has roiled the final days of one the nation’s most closely watched races.
Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, in a race that is among a handful expected to determine which party controls the Senate for the final two year’s of Trump’s term.
Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name. It was that candidate’s presence on the ballot that prompted Trump to push for the lawsuit out of fear he would siphon votes from the incumbent.
Trending
Shortly after the ruling, the Justice Department filed a notice saying it was appealing: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and as early voting was underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the order that the relief the federal government seeks is “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argued that the case lacked any legal basis and amounted to election interference.
“Today’s ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don’t like the result,” said the committee’s executive director, Devan Barber.
The Justice Department, attorneys for the state and Peltola’s campaign did not immediately return messages seeking comment.
Senator says he expects ‘to lose a lot of votes’ to the other Dan Sullivan
The senator and his allies, including Trump, for months have portrayed Dan J. Sullivan as a sham candidate intent on confusing voters and helping Peltola.
Earlier Sunday, Sen. Sullivan told CNN that he thought the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot would affect the election.
“I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery,” he said.
He also said he doubted claims by Peltola that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters.
“There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” Sullivan told CNN’s “State of the Union.” “She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us.”
The senator’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Sunday court ruling.
In the week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in efforts to recruit the second Sullivan. Shortly after entering the race in June, Dan J. Sullivan said he’d had no contact with her campaign about running. He has not responded to multiple messages over the past few days.
His recent public absence prompted a social media post Sunday by the president: “The Fake Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., has DISAPPEARED! Nobody can find him, including Law Enforcement.”
Peltola’s campaign responded to the Times story by saying it had no involvement in the campaigns for either Sullivan: “I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said during a recent campaign event.
In its statement indicating its plans to appeal, the Justice Department said the federal judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the government’s argument that Dan J. Sullivan entered the race “as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”
Multiple investigations look into whether Dan J. Sullivan was recruited as a decoy candidate
State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected an earlier Republican-backed effort to block the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot on which he appeared as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Both Sullivans appear the same way on the general election ballot. Peltola placed first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan received about 2.5% of the primary vote, but that was enough to finish within the top four and qualify for the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election.
Attorneys for the Alaska Department of Law represented state elections officials in the case and asked Gleason, who was appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama, to toss the lawsuit. They filed a scathing response to the federal government’s complaint, calling it “meritless.”
Alaska also said the state had taken “significant steps” to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. Voters who still might be confused could ask for help or look up candidate biographies and other information in state-distributed election pamphlets.
Republicans, including ones working with Trump, also have a long history of backing decoy candidates in elections. The governor, a Republican, has ordered an investigation and suggested he may not certify a possible Peltola victory.
In her ruling, Gleason wrote that the Trump administration’s attempt to block certification ran counter to the Constitution, which gives states the authority to run elections. She also cited the Supreme Court’s Purcell principle, which holds that federal courts should generally not change election rules too close to an election.
Kristen Clarke, general counsel of the NAACP, which had filed a brief supporting the case’s dismissal, called the judge’s decision “a big win for the voters in Alaska.”
“The law is clear, and the DOJ’s case was a baseless, eleventh hour attempt to hijack this midterm election,” she said.
On Thursday, the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation over the presence of Dan J. Sullivan on the Alaska ballot, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. The FBI also has begun contacting people who donated to him, some of whom told the AP that the agents were asking if they had been misled about which candidate they were supporting.
___
Riccardi reported from Washington. Associated Press photographer Lindsey Wasson in Anchorage, Alaska, and AP writer Ali Swenson in Washington contributed to this report.
This is a developing story and has been updated with a comment from President Trump.

Obama Judge Kills DOJ Bid to Probe Alaska ‘Decoy Dan’ Scheme Just Two Days Before Election
An Obama-appointed federal judge threw out the Trump Justice Department’s lawsuit on Sunday aimed at stopping certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses because of votes siphoned by a same-named spoiler
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason, named to the bench by Barack Obama, ruled the government lacked standing and offered no workable way to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan without shredding voter secrecy. She also called the request infeasible with early voting already well underway and Election Day just two days off.
The DOJ suit, filed at President Trump’s direction less than two weeks ago, targeted the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan—a retired teacher from Petersburg—on the ballot alongside Sen. Dan Sullivan. The department argued the second Sullivan entered the race to confuse voters and potentially flip a tight contest against Democrat Mary Peltola. 
A New York Times report had detailed how operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit him. The complaint sought an investigation into voter intent and a hold on certifying any result the decoy could have swung.
Gleason shut it down on procedural grounds. She wrote that the United States provided “no workable plan” for segregating those ballots and then running an investigation while protecting the secret ballot. She added that ordering such a move would itself create confusion and keep people from the polls. Alaska election officials, backed by the GOP-led state government, had called the case meritless and said voters already had tools to tell the two candidates apart. 
The DOJ immediately appealed, with a spokesperson stating that Alaskan voters “deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes.” The court dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the core claim that Daniel J. Sullivan ran as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.
This lands in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country, where control of the chamber could hang in the balance. Sen. Sullivan has said the second name on the ballot will cost him votes to “trickery.” Separate criminal and civil probes into the recruitment effort remain active. With ballots already cast and the clock ticking, the ruling leaves the alleged confusion scheme unaddressed before votes are counted.

A federal judge on Sunday rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to block certification of the Alaska Senate election results before the vote.
The ruling dealt a significant setback to the administration just two days before the November 3 midterm elections.
The Justice Department argued that Daniel J. Sullivan, whom the Trump administration has labeled “Decoy Dan,” had entered the race as a “frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”
“Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” the DOJ said in its filing.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled that the Trump administration lacked standing to bring the lawsuit. The case sought to compel Alaska to separate ballots if Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan lost his reelection campaign to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola.
The Justice Department is appealing the decision, although it remains unclear whether any significant action will be possible before Election Day on Tuesday, November 3.
The Senate contest has drawn unusual national attention in recent weeks after reports that Daniel J. Sullivan, a Republican whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent, may have entered the race as a spoiler candidate in an effort to divide Republican support.
In its lawsuit, the Justice Department argued that the second Sullivan’s campaign was intended to “dupe Alaska’s voters into believing that he is Senator Sullivan.” The department asked the court to segregate the ballots if Peltola won. But Gleason said Sunday that doing so would be impossible without violating voters’ right to privacy and the secrecy of the ballot.

Win for Voters: Judge Throws Out DOJ Bid to Subvert Alaska Election
In win for voters, judge throws out DOJ bid to subvert Alaska election
In a major win for voters, a federal judge Sunday threw out the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) bid to undermine Alaska’s U.S. Senate race through an eleventh-hour lawsuit.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason, appointed by President Barack Obama, dismissed the Justice Department’s bid to stop Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election if the GOP candidate loses. The state also cannot be forced to keep and segregate ballots of those who cast a vote for independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan, Gleason ruled.
“The Court cannot grant the United States the relief it seeks,” Gleason wrote, finding that DOJ failed to explain how its proposed remedy could work while preserving Alaska voters’ right to a secret ballot.
Gleason said DOJ offered “no workable plan” for separating ballots and then investigating whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan actually intended to support incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
“Requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order,” Gleason wrote, saying it would violate Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot.
Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.
The lawsuit was yet another attempt by the Trump administration to interfere in states’ constitutional power to administer elections. Alaska is a key battleground state in determining the control of the U.S. Senate.
The DOJ had argued any votes “impacted by voter confusion” should be set aside because the Republican and independent candidate share a first and last name. However, Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system that allows voters to rank more than one candidate. To avoid any confusion, the ballot also identifies the candidates’ party and clearly labels Sen. Sullivan as the incumbent.
Gleason also rejected DOJ’s contention that its requested relief would not interfere with Alaska’s election administration.
“These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska’s election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the executive branch of the federal government,” she wrote.
The state election board, along with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, Senate Democrats* and voting advocates, had asked the judge to toss out the lawsuit, arguing it failed to state an actionable claim. They argued the government’s claims under the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) were faulty and exceeded the authority granted to the executive branch by Congress.
Gleason dismissed the lawsuit for lack of standing and denied DOJ leave to amend, finding that another rewrite would be futile because the court lacks authority to order ballots segregated for a federal law-enforcement investigation into voters’ intent.
*The Elias Law Group (ELG) represents the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in this case. ELG Firm Chair Marc Elias is the founder of Democracy Docket.
